explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, is the one Paul means. The glory on his face was so strong that the Israelites could not gaze at it. Exodus 34:30 says they were afraid to come near him once they saw his face was radiant. That's a lot to carry around, friend, and he didn't even have a flashlight.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), and he's a fair guess. But Paul names Moses here, and it's Moses' face that Israel couldn't gaze at. Exodus 34:30 says Aaron and all the Israelites saw that Moses' face was radiant, and they were afraid to come near him. So Aaron was standing right there, just not the one glowing.

Joshua was Moses' attendant (Exodus 24:13), so he's a good name to reach for. But Paul says it was the face of Moses that the Israelites could not gaze at. Joshua isn't mentioned in these verses at all. This one belongs to Moses, friend.

Paul actually calls it a "fleeting glory," so it wasn't there to stay. He says the ministry of death came with glory, but that glory was on its way out. Moses had it on his face, and Paul says it was fading. Impressive, yes. Permanent, no.

You picked it right, friend. Paul says the glory on Moses' face was a "fleeting glory." It was real and it was bright, but it was on its way out. Paul says the same thing again in verse 13, calling it "…what was fading away…"

That's exactly what Paul says. He asks, "…will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?" He's building on the glory of the ministry of death and saying the ministry of the Spirit goes past it. He doesn't whisper it either, friend. He says it with his whole chest.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He asks, "…will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?" The ministry of death came with glory, and he says the ministry of the Spirit is more glorious than that. He's stacking glory on top of glory.

Righteousness is the word Paul uses. He says that if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, "…how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!" Condemnation on one side, righteousness on the other. And Paul says the second one has the greater glory.

It sounds close to condemnation, so I get why it jumped out. But the word Paul sets against condemnation is righteousness. He says, "…how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!" Judgment doesn't show up in this verse.

Sacrifice is a big word all over the Bible, but it's not the one in this verse. Paul sets the ministry of condemnation next to the ministry of righteousness. He says the ministry of righteousness is much more glorious. Sacrifice didn't make this particular guest list.

Paul says what was fading away came with glory, and then he says, "…how much greater is the glory of that which endures!" One glory was fading, and the other lasts. And he says the one that lasts is the greater glory. That's the difference between a batch that cools off on the counter and a batch that stays warm.

Close, but that's not how Paul puts it. He calls the first glory "…what was fading away…" For the greater glory he says it's "…that which endures!" Fading and enduring are the two sides he sets against each other.

Paul doesn't say the greater glory is sitting around waiting. He says it is "…the glory of that which endures!" That's the word he uses, and it's set against what was fading away. The glory that lasts is the greater one.
You got it, baker. Paul says, "…since we have such a hope, we are very bold." The hope comes first and the boldness follows. He doesn't say they're bold because they feel brave on a Monday morning.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold." The hope is what he points to, and the boldness comes with it. He and those with him are very bold.

Paul says Moses "…would put a veil over his face…" Exodus 34:33 says the same, that Moses put a veil over his face. Paul brings it up because it connects to what he says next about the old covenant. A veil is simply a covering, friend, and that one went on his face.

A turban is a fair guess for something on a head, but Paul doesn't say that. He says Moses "…would put a veil over his face…" Exodus 34:33 also says Moses put a veil over his face. So it's a veil, and it covered the face.
A helmet would've been a bold look, friend, but it's not in the text. Paul says Moses "…would put a veil over his face…" Exodus 34:33 says that too. A veil is what he used.

explanations.answer: So they wouldn't see the end of what was fading
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. Moses would put a veil over his face "…to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away." The glory on his face was fading, and the veil kept them from gazing at the end of it. I think that's a lot like covering a cookie tray with a towel so nobody watches the last of the steam rise. Paul gives the reason himself, so we can take it straight from him.

explanations.answer: So they would listen to Aaron instead of him
explanations.explanation: Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but Paul never brings him up here. The reason Paul gives is that Moses put the veil on "…to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away." Nothing in these verses says it was about who they listened to. It was about the fading glory.

explanations.answer: So he could rest from speaking to them
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about Moses needing a break. He says Moses would put a veil over his face "…to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away." That's the reason he gives. I'd leave the rest out, friend, since the text doesn't say it.

Paul says the veil "…has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed." It's not removed by trying harder, and it's not removed by reading it again. He says it's only in Christ. My mustache can't lift that veil, friend, and neither can anyone else's.

Abraham is the man God called to leave his country (Genesis 12:1), so he's an important name. But Paul says the veil can be removed "…only in Christ…" Abraham isn't mentioned in these verses at all. The answer is Christ, and Paul says only in Him.

Elijah the prophet (1 Kings 18:36) is a big name in the Bible, but he's not in this passage. Paul says the veil "…has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed." So the answer is Christ. Elijah will have to wait for another batch.
Hearts is the word Paul uses. He says, "…even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts." He's not talking about a cloth on someone's face here. The covering is over their hearts.

Eyes is a natural guess, since a veil sounds like something you'd see through. But Paul says, "…a veil covers their hearts." He says it covers their hearts, not their eyes. That's the word in the verse.
Moses is being read here, so ears is a reasonable guess. But Paul says, "…when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts." The veil is over their hearts. Ears didn't make it into the verse.

explanations.answer: Whenever anyone turns to the Lord
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "…whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away." Notice the word "anyone." He doesn't set a limit on who can turn. And when someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

That's actually where Paul says the veil stays. He says, "…even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts." Reading Moses again is where the veil remains, and turning to the Lord is where it's taken away. Hearing Moses read doesn't lift it, friend. Turning to the Lord does.

explanations.answer: Whenever the old glory fades out
explanations.explanation: Paul does say the old glory was fading, but he doesn't say that's what takes the veil away. He says, "…whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away." The turning to the Lord is the moment he points to.

Paul says, "…where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." He just said the veil is taken away when anyone turns to the Lord. Now he says where the Spirit of the Lord is, there's freedom. That's a good place to stand, friend.
Quiet sounds nice, especially after a long day in the bakery. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says, "…where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." The word is freedom.
Order is a good word, and I'm a fan of a tidy cooling rack myself. But it's not what Paul says. He writes, "…where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Freedom is the word in the verse.

explanations.answer: We are being transformed into His image
explanations.explanation: Paul says those of us who reflect the glory of the Lord with unveiled faces "…are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory…" Notice it's "are being." It's happening now, and it keeps going. And he says the glory comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

explanations.answer: We are being sent out to all nations
explanations.explanation: "Sent out to all nations" sounds like a full tray of good news, friend, and I almost grabbed it myself. But this verse isn't about where we go. Paul says all of us who reflect the glory of the Lord with unveiled faces "…are being transformed into His image…" So we reflect His glory and we're changed into His image, with a glory that's "intensifying," not fading like the glory on Moses' face. Nobody here is packing a suitcase.

explanations.answer: We are being given a new name
explanations.explanation: A new name would be exciting, but it's not what Paul says in these verses. He says we "…are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory…" The change is into His image. No name change is mentioned.

Paul says the fading belongs to the glory on Moses' face (2 Corinthians 3:7). About the glory we reflect, he says we "…are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit." He doesn't say that glory fades. So the statement puts the fading in the wrong place.

You've got it, baker. The fading belongs to the glory on Moses' face. Paul says we "…are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit." It's an intensifying glory, so it grows instead of fading.
